title: EDTA Powder (Detergent Grade)
description: Ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) — chelating agent for water hardness control, metal sequestration, and stability enhancement in detergent, cleaning, and industrial formulations.

details.longDescription:
EDTA (ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid, CAS 60-00-4) is the workhorse chelating agent of detergent and cleaning chemistry. Global Chemicals LLC supplies it from stock in Muscat in 25 kg bags as the two sodium salts formulators use: disodium EDTA (EDTA-2Na, CAS 6381-92-6, 99% minimum, pH 4–5 in 1% solution) for neutral and mildly acidic products, and tetrasodium EDTA (EDTA-4Na, CAS 64-02-8, 99% minimum, pH 10.5–11.5) for alkaline liquids and powders. Food-grade calcium disodium EDTA (E385) is available on request, and the laboratory grade is listed under laboratory chemicals.

What it does. EDTA binds calcium, magnesium, iron, copper and manganese ions into stable, water-soluble complexes so they cannot react with anything else. One kilogram of tetrasodium EDTA (anhydrous basis) sequesters about 260 g of hardness expressed as calcium carbonate. In liquid and powder detergents at 0.1–2% it stops hard water forming soap scum and precipitating surfactant, so the product cleans in Oman's hard municipal and well water as it does in soft water; in bleaches it chelates the trace iron and copper that catalyse the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide and hypochlorite, extending shelf life; in cosmetics and personal care at 0.05–0.2% it boosts preservatives and keeps formulations clear; in industrial cleaners, boiler and heat-exchanger descalers and CIP acids it dissolves iron and scale deposits; and in water treatment it controls iron and manganese that would stain and foul.

Choosing the salt. Tetrasodium EDTA dissolves fastest and matches the pH of alkaline detergents and degreasers; disodium EDTA suits neutral shampoos, cosmetics and acidic descalers and is the lab titrant. Both are stable powders that dissolve readily; raise the pH with caustic if a strong disodium solution is slow to clear. EDTA is persistent in the environment, so formulators selling into markets that require readily biodegradable chelants can ask us about GLDA and MGDA alternatives.

Storage and handling: keep bags closed and dry; the dust is harmful if inhaled and the tetrasodium salt can cause serious eye damage, so avoid raising dust and wear gloves, goggles and a dust mask. Every lot carries a certificate of analysis giving assay, pH and chelation value, and a GHS safety data sheet.

title: Glycerine (Soap & Personal Care Grade)
description: Pharmaceutical/technical grade glycerine (glycerol) — humectant, solvent, and plasticiser for soap, cosmetics, food, pharmaceutical, and industrial applications in Oman.

details.longDescription:
Glycerine (glycerol, glycerin, C3H8O3, CAS 56-81-5) is a clear, colourless, practically odourless and sweet-tasting viscous liquid. Global Chemicals LLC supplies it from stock in Muscat as refined pharmaceutical grade (99.5% minimum, USP/BP), food grade (E422) and technical grade, in 250 kg drums and 1,250 kg IBCs, to soap and cosmetic makers, food processors, pharmaceutical plants and industrial users across Oman and the GCC.

Which grade. USP/BP glycerine is the refined product with water at 0.5% maximum and ash at 10 ppm maximum; it is the grade for medicines, cosmetics, toothpaste and any product applied to skin or swallowed, and it ships with a certificate of analysis against the pharmacopoeia. Food grade (E422) carries food-safety documentation for confectionery, bakery and beverage use. Technical grade suits uses where purity is secondary: antifreeze and heat-transfer blends, resins and alkyds, textile and paper processing, and as a plasticiser or lubricant.

In soap and personal care glycerine is the main humectant: it draws water into the skin and holds it, which is why it sits in lotions, creams, shaving products, hand sanitisers and liquid soaps. In bar soap it keeps bars from cracking, and transparent and melt-and-pour soaps rely heavily on it. In food it keeps cakes, fillings and confectionery moist, sweetens without sugar and carries flavours and colours. In pharmaceuticals it is a vehicle and co-solvent in cough syrups and oral solutions, and the base of glycerin suppositories, ear drops and topical gels.

Handling and storage. Glycerine is not classed as hazardous for transport, but it is hygroscopic, so keep drums and IBCs closed to stop it absorbing water and drifting off specification. It thickens markedly when cold; warm it gently before pumping rather than heating it hard. Keep it away from strong oxidisers such as potassium permanganate and concentrated nitric acid, with which it can react violently. A safety data sheet and certificate of analysis come with every delivery.

details.longDescription:
Hydrogen peroxide 50% (H2O2, CAS 7722-84-1) is a clear, colourless oxidiser supplied at 50% w/w (±0.5%), specific gravity 1.196 at 20 °C, stabilised to pH 1–4 with a non-volatile residue below 60 ppm. Why 50% rather than 35%: one kilogram of the 50% grade carries the active oxygen of 1.43 kg of 35%, so large users store, transport and dose less liquid for the same duty. Diluting with demineralised water gives any working strength; tap water with iron or copper will decompose the peroxide. It breaks down to water and oxygen only, which is why it replaces chlorine-based bleaches wherever halogenated by-products are a concern.

Industrial uses in Oman: high-brightness bleaching of pulp, paper, textiles and nonwovens in alkaline baths; chemical synthesis (epoxidation, hydroxylation and other oxidations); COD and BOD reduction in effluent, including Fenton treatment with ferrous iron for refractory organics; sulphide and mercaptan oxidation in oil and gas produced water; in-situ chemical oxidation of contaminated soil and groundwater; electronics cleaning; and oxidative leaching in mineral processing. Dosing is by the oxygen demand of the stream, confirmed with a residual-peroxide test.

Handling: hydrogen peroxide 50% is a Class 5.1 oxidiser with a Class 8 corrosive subsidiary hazard (UN 2014), and it causes serious burns to skin and eyes. Keep it in its original vented containers, in the shade, away from metals, organics, acids and reducing agents; contamination, heat or metal ions trigger decomposition that releases oxygen and heat, so never return unused product to the drum and never store it in a sealed, unvented vessel. Transfer with passivated stainless steel, aluminium or HDPE equipment only, and wear chemical goggles, gloves and a face shield. A GHS safety data sheet and handling guide come with every delivery, together with a certificate of analysis.

title: LABSA
description: Linear Alkylbenzene Sulphonic Acid (LABSA 96%) — the primary anionic surfactant raw material for liquid detergent, dish wash, laundry, and industrial cleaner production in Oman and GCC.

details.longDescription:
LABSA (linear alkylbenzene sulphonic acid, CAS 27176-87-0) is the raw material behind most liquid detergents. Global Chemicals LLC supplies the 96% grade from stock in Muscat in 200 kg HDPE drums and 1,000 kg IBCs to detergent manufacturers, cleaning-product formulators and industrial blenders across Oman and the GCC: a dark brown, viscous liquid with 96% minimum active matter, 0.5–2.0% free sulphuric acid, 2.0–4.0% unsulphonated material, Klett colour 40–60, specific gravity 1.05–1.06 and a flash point above 100 °C.

How it is used. LABSA is an acid and is never used as such in a product; it is neutralised to sodium linear alkylbenzene sulphonate (SLAS or LAS), the anionic surfactant that does the cleaning and foaming. Neutralising 1 kg of LABSA takes about 125 g of sodium hydroxide, which is roughly 250 g of 50% caustic solution, to reach pH 7–8; add the acid slowly to the water and caustic with good stirring, because the reaction gives off heat, and finish the pH with a little acid or caustic. The resulting paste or solution is then built into the product: dish-wash liquids at 10–20% LAS with SLES and a foam booster, liquid laundry detergents, all-purpose and floor cleaners, car shampoos, toilet-bowl cleaners and industrial degreasers. Soda ash or triethanolamine can replace caustic where the formulation calls for them. Outside cleaning, LAS is an emulsifier in agrochemical formulations and a wetting agent in textile and leather processing.

Why LABSA: it is the lowest-cost surfactant per unit of cleaning, it is readily biodegradable in its linear form, it tolerates hard water when built with a chelant, and it blends with every common co-surfactant. The FAQs on this page give the standard ratios.

Handling: LABSA is a strong acid that burns skin and eyes and attacks mild steel; store it in HDPE, stainless or lined tanks, keep drums closed and out of the sun to limit colour darkening, and wear gloves, goggles and a face shield. It is not classed as a flammable liquid, but it is combustible. Every delivery carries a certificate of analysis giving active matter, free acid, unsulphonated matter and colour, a technical data sheet, formulation guidance and a GHS safety data sheet.

faqs.question: What is LABSA and how is it used in detergent manufacturing in Oman?
faqs.answer: LABSA (Linear Alkyl Benzene Sulphonic Acid, CAS 27176-87-0) is the world's most widely used synthetic surfactant and the primary raw material for manufacturing household and industrial detergents. In Oman's detergent production sector and soap manufacturing industry, LABSA is neutralised with sodium hydroxide (caustic soda) or triethanolamine to produce the corresponding sulphonate salt, which is the active cleaning ingredient in laundry powders, dishwashing liquids, floor cleaners, and industrial detergents. The resulting linear alkyl benzene sulphonate (LAS) provides excellent hard-surface cleaning, high foam generation, and good compatibility with other surfactants. LABSA at 96% active content is the standard commercial grade — it must be handled and stored above 10°C as it solidifies below this temperature, which is occasionally relevant in Oman's winter months in interior regions. LABSA is readily biodegradable (>90% in 28 days), making LAS-based detergents preferred over branched-chain surfactants from an environmental perspective. Global Chemicals LLC supplies LABSA in drums, IBCs, and bulk tankers for Oman's detergent manufacturers.

faqs.question: What is the correct ratio of LABSA to caustic soda for making liquid detergent?
faqs.answer: The neutralisation ratio of LABSA to caustic soda (sodium hydroxide) depends on the specific LABSA active content and the desired sulphonate concentration. For LABSA at 96% active content (the standard commercial grade), the stoichiometric ratio is approximately 1.3 kg of 98% caustic soda flakes per 10 kg of LABSA to achieve complete neutralisation to sodium linear alkyl benzene sulphonate (SLAS) at pH 7–9. In practice, a slight excess of caustic soda (5–10% over stoichiometric) is used to ensure complete neutralisation and produce a slightly alkaline final product (pH 9–10), which improves cleaning performance and product stability. The neutralisation reaction is exothermic — in Oman's ambient temperatures, the heat generated can raise the temperature to 50–60°C; mixing should be done in a vessel with water cooling capability. For liquid detergent formulation at 15% active content, the LABSA-caustic paste is diluted with water and other ingredients (SLES co-surfactant, salt for viscosity, fragrance, preservative). Global Chemicals LLC provides LABSA with technical support for detergent formulation.

faqs.question: What is sodium tripolyphosphate (STPP) and why is it used in detergents?
faqs.answer: Sodium tripolyphosphate (STPP, pentasodium triphosphate, CAS 7758-29-4) is a phosphate builder used in heavy-duty laundry and dishwashing detergents to improve cleaning performance. It functions through three complementary mechanisms: water softening (STPP chelates calcium and magnesium ions in hard water, preventing them from deactivating the surfactant and depositing as insoluble soap scum), sequestration (maintains calcium and magnesium in solution throughout the wash cycle, preventing redeposition on fabric), and soil suspension (STPP's alkaline buffering action and peptisation of protein and clay soils improves soil release from fabric). Oman's water supply from groundwater sources has high hardness (200–500 mg/L as CaCO₃), making phosphate builders valuable for laundry performance. However, environmental concerns about eutrophication (phosphate in wastewater stimulates algal growth in freshwater bodies) have driven many markets towards zeolite and citrate-based phosphate-free alternatives. In Oman and the Gulf, phosphate-containing detergents remain in use. Global Chemicals LLC supplies STPP in powder form for Oman's detergent manufacturing and industrial cleaning sectors.
